edges.rationale: CSMA/CA, random backoff, and link-layer ACKs operate on the shared channel within a BSS; understanding APs, channels, and the overlapping-AP 'WiFi jungle' is needed to see why collision avoidance (not detection) and ACKs are used.
The frame's address fields and the exchange of frames between a wireless host and an AP presuppose the BSS/AP model, channel usage, and the association relationship covered in the architecture topic.
Control and management frame types and the host–AP frame exchange sequence (e.g., acknowledgments) only make sense once the CSMA/CA access and acknowledgment procedure is understood.

edges.dependent: Mobility in the Same IP Subnet
edges.rationale: Handover between APs in a subnet is an extension of the initial association process across overlapping BSSs; association, AP roles, and the WiFi jungle must be learned first.

edges.dependent: Mobility in the Same IP Subnet
edges.rationale: Reassociation during handover is carried out via 802.11 management frames; knowing frame types and addressing clarifies what is exchanged when a station moves between APs.
Power management (stations dozing while APs buffer frames) and other advanced capabilities are defined in terms of station–AP interactions within a BSS.
Rate adaptation relies on transmission outcomes observed through the MAC procedure (missing ACKs, backoff behavior), so CSMA/CA is needed to understand how and why transmission rates are adjusted.
